thesis: Position update, not a new idea: DKS was opened 2026-11-13 at 144.50 and the 2026-11-24 Q3 print confirmed the thesis rather than changing it, closing +14.59% at 153.17. Net sales rose 23.2% to $5.13bn, the DICK'S comp was +2.6%, and critically the Foot Locker comp turned positive at +0.5% proforma, which is the integration bet working; management raised FY26 non-GAAP EPS guidance to $11.45-12.30 from $11.00-12.00, putting the stock at 12.9x the new midpoint with a $1.25 quarterly dividend declared (3.3% yield).
key_risk: Non-GAAP EPS of $1.94 was DOWN from $2.07 a year ago and gross margin fell to 32.40% from 33.13% — the growth is acquired, not organic, and Foot Locker full-year comp guidance is still negative 2.0% to 0.0%. The stock is 37.3% off its 244.38 range high for that reason. A post-earnings gap of this size also frequently fills.
counter_argument: The strongest case against holding is that the easy money is made: at 153.17 the remaining run to 175.50 is +14.6% while the 129.00 stop is 15.8% below, so the forward reward-to-risk from today is roughly 0.9:1 even though it is 2.0:1 from the original entry. The counter is that 129.00 is 2.0 ATR from entry and is the minimum honest stop width per config/strategy.md; tightening it to flatter the ratio is exactly the KRE failure documented in CLAUDE.md, and the alternative to a wide stop is trimming size, not moving the level.

thesis: Not a bet on the consumer — a bet on a founder-forced product reset in a name where expectations have already capitulated. Chip Wilson holds 8.6% (9,570,851 shares, 13D/A Amendment 25) and under a 2026-05-26 cooperation agreement the board was expanded from twelve to thirteen on 2026-10-19 to seat Tara Poseley, who was lululemon's own Chief Product Officer from 2013-2015 — the appointment targets precisely the product and brand-momentum failure that took the stock 44.9% off its high. Sell-side positioning is washed out at 4.8% bullish (1 strong buy, 1 buy, 31 hold, 6 sell, 3 strong sell), yet the company beat consensus in three of its last four quarters, including by 12.5% last quarter.
key_risk: Earnings gap risk is the live danger: ATR14 is 4.45%, so a disappointing 2026-12-09 print can gap straight through the 95.50 stop overnight rather than filling it, which is why this is sized at 2%. Beyond that, this is consumer discretionary bought into a Fed tightening cycle, analyst revisions are still deteriorating (strong sell 2 to 3 over four months), and at 106.05 the stock remains 16.7% below its 127.31 SMA200 — the long-term trend is still down and a governance fix takes quarters to show up in comps.
counter_argument: The strongest case against is my own macro work: I concluded this morning that the Fed is hiking into a weakening consumer and that the right posture is defensive, which argues against owning premium athleisure at all. The answer is that LULU is already 44.9% off its high and 16.7% below its 200-day average, so the consumer-cycle risk is substantially in the price — unlike DG and KR, which I rejected today precisely because they sit within 4% of their highs and leave no room for an honest stop. The second counter, that a 4.8% bullish share means the Street knows something, cuts both ways: it is also why a modest beat re-rates the stock hard, and the fetched record shows three beats in four quarters.

thesis: The one name found today that is in an actual uptrend while the index is not: GIII closed 31.69, above its SMA20 (31.39), SMA50 (29.25) and SMA200 (31.03) simultaneously, on a session when SPY and QQQ both sat below their 20- and 50-day averages and SMH fell 7.26%. Chairman and CEO Morris Goldfarb bought 40,000 shares on the open market at $27.94 on 2026-09-14 ($1.12m) and there have been zero insider sales in six months, which is the single most predictive public signal available and it is here in a name the market has not re-rated. Average dollar volume is $12.3m on 387,478 shares a day, so this is a small cap and must be sized as one.
key_risk: Liquidity and gap risk together: at $12.3m average daily dollar volume this is a thin small cap, so a position must stay a small fraction of a day's trade and an exit in a panic will cost spread — which is why it is 2%, not 3%. G-III is a wholesaler of licensed brands (DKNY, Karl Lagerfeld, plus Calvin Klein and Tommy Hilfiger licences), so it carries both department-store channel risk and licence-renewal risk, and its surprise record includes a -49.94% miss in the quarter to 2026-03-31 — this company can and does miss badly. Apparel is also discretionary consumer spending bought into a Fed tightening cycle.
counter_argument: The strongest case against is that analyst coverage is thin (10 analysts, revisions dead flat for four straight months at 70% bullish), so there is no revision momentum to carry the stock and a single downgrade moves it hard. The honest answer is that flat thin coverage is the condition under which an insider signal carries the most information rather than the least — nobody has marked this name up or down, and the person with the best view of the order book put $1.12m of his own money in at $27.94 and has not sold any. That is a different and better reason to own it than a sell-side upgrade cycle.
